idiom_name: DRF permission classes (BasePermission.has_permission / has_object_permission) on the view
implementation_notes: The framework runs the check for you, so the classic enforcer becomes a permission class: view-level rules implement has_permission(self, request, view), object-level rules implement has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj), and the classes are listed in permission_classes (or DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES); a failure raises PermissionDenied or NotAuthenticated before the view body runs. Object checks are applied automatically only by generic views through get_object()/check_object_permissions(), so a custom view must call it explicitly - and because list endpoints and create never call get_object(), filtering the queryset and performing the create check in the serializer or perform_create() is part of the enforcement. FastAPI and Django use the same shape with security dependencies and PermissionRequiredMixin/user_passes_test; all rules belong in those classes, not in view bodies.
pitfalls: Object-level permissions do not run for list endpoints or on create (get_object() is never called): restrict creation in perform_create()/the serializer and scope querysets explicitly.
The default DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES is AllowAny, so a view that forgets permission_classes is open; set a deny-by-default global policy.
A permission that returns a truthy object or catches PermissionDenied instead of returning False turns the decision into a silent allow.
